name: Patterns and automation
description: Decisions as patterns, flows, and measuring the machine share.

cards.subject: A workflow
says: chains steps into a repeatable process that runs without a person driving each one
has a defined trigger, ordered steps and an end state
cards.use: want a multi-step process to run the same way every time
not: is a single function call that cannot be split into steps

cards.subject: A trigger
says: starts a workflow when something happens or a time arrives
is the entry point of a workflow rather than one of its actions
cards.use: need to define what causes a workflow to begin
not: decides which branch runs after the first step

cards.subject: A step
says: does one unit of work inside a workflow
passes its output to later steps as their input
cards.use: need to break a process into units that can be retried separately
not: is the whole workflow rather than a part of it

cards.subject: A condition
says: routes a workflow down one path based on the data it sees
evaluates a rule such as an order total above a limit
cards.use: need large and small requests to be handled differently
not: runs every branch at once regardless of the data

cards.subject: A fan-out and fan-in
says: splits work into parallel branches and later joins their results
can wait for every branch, or only a quorum, before continuing
cards.use: need to process many items at once and then combine the outcomes
not: sends work to one branch at a time in a fixed order

cards.subject: A state machine
says: allows only declared transitions between named states
makes an illegal move such as completed back to running impossible
cards.use: need to guarantee that a task never lands in an impossible state
not: lets any state change to any other state freely

cards.subject: A saga
says: undoes completed steps with compensating actions when a later step fails
replaces one distributed transaction with a sequence of local ones
cards.use: need all-or-nothing behaviour across services that share no transaction
not: locks every service's database until the whole process commits

cards.subject: Orchestration
says: has one central coordinator tell each service what to do next
keeps the whole process visible and changeable in one place
cards.use: need the end-to-end flow to be readable in a single definition
not: lets each service react on its own with no coordinator

cards.subject: Choreography
says: lets each service react to events with no central coordinator
spreads the process definition across many subscribers
cards.use: want services to stay loosely coupled and react on their own
not: depends on a single engine that calls every step in turn

cards.subject: A long-running workflow
says: persists its state between steps so it survives restarts
can wait days for a timer or a person without holding a thread
cards.use: have a process that waits days for an outside answer
not: must finish inside a single request timeout

cards.subject: A background job
says: runs work outside the request that asked for it
lets a web request return before slow work finishes
cards.use: need a slow task not to block the user's page
not: must complete before the user gets any response

cards.subject: A job queue
says: holds jobs until a worker is free to take them
decouples how fast jobs arrive from how fast they are processed
cards.use: see bursts of work arriving faster than it can be done
not: runs each job at the moment it is added, never later

cards.subject: A worker
says: pulls jobs from a queue and executes them
can be scaled out by running more copies
cards.use: need more throughput from the same queue
not: decides which jobs are created

cards.subject: An acknowledgement
says: tells the queue that a job finished so it can be removed
is safest sent after the work is durably done
cards.use: need a crash mid-job not to lose the job
not: is sent before the work starts to speed things up

cards.subject: A concurrency limit
says: caps how many jobs of one kind run at once
protects a downstream system from being overwhelmed
cards.use: need to stop a bulk import from exhausting a database connection pool
not: raises throughput by letting unlimited jobs run together

cards.subject: A visibility timeout
says: hides a claimed job from other workers for a limited time
returns the job to the queue if the worker never acknowledges it
cards.use: need a crashed worker's job to be picked up by another worker
not: deletes a job that takes too long to run

cards.subject: A job heartbeat
says: extends a running job's claim while its worker is still alive
lets a long job outlive the normal claim time without being run twice
cards.use: run a job that takes far longer than the claim period
not: marks the job completed when it is sent

cards.subject: Backpressure
says: slows or rejects producers when consumers fall behind
keeps an unbounded queue from exhausting memory
cards.use: see queue depth growing without limit
not: adds more producers to catch up with the backlog

cards.subject: An event
says: records that something has already happened
is usually named in the past tense, like invoice.paid
cards.use: need to announce a fact that other systems may care about
not: orders one particular service to perform an action

cards.subject: A command
says: asks one specific recipient to do something
can be rejected by the recipient
cards.use: need a particular service to carry out an action
not: announces a fact to anyone who is listening

cards.subject: A producer
says: emits events without knowing who will consume them
is unaffected when a new consumer is added
cards.use: need the sender to stay independent of the receivers
not: must call every consumer directly

cards.subject: A consumer
says: receives events it registered interest in
can be added without changing the producer
cards.use: want to react to something another system did
not: decides what the producer publishes

cards.subject: A message broker
says: stores and routes messages between producers and consumers
buffers events while a consumer is down
cards.use: need events to survive a consumer outage
not: executes the business logic of every consumer

cards.subject: Pub/sub
says: delivers one published message to every subscriber of a topic
differs from a work queue where each message goes to one worker
cards.use: need several systems to each react to the same event
not: gives each message to exactly one worker that competes for it

cards.subject: A thin event
says: carries only an identifier and makes the consumer fetch the details
keeps messages small and the data always current
cards.use: want small events and always-fresh data
not: carries the full record so no callback is ever needed

cards.subject: A fat event
says: carries the full state consumers need
saves consumers a callback to the producer
cards.use: want consumers to work even if the producer is unreachable
not: carries only an identifier

cards.subject: Event ordering
says: is guaranteed only within a partition or key in most brokers
needs a key or sequence number when changes must be applied in order
cards.use: must apply updates to the same account in the order they happened
not: is guaranteed globally across all topics by default

cards.subject: The transactional outbox
says: writes the event to a table in the same transaction as the state change
uses a relay to publish the stored rows afterwards
cards.use: find that a service saved data but crashed before publishing the event
not: publishes first and saves the state later

cards.subject: Event sourcing
says: stores state as an append-only sequence of events
rebuilds current state by replaying those events
cards.use: need a complete history of every change to an aggregate
not: keeps only the latest value and overwrites it on each change

cards.subject: A webhook
says: is an HTTP callback the sender makes when an event occurs
removes the need for the receiver to poll
cards.use: want to be told about changes instead of asking repeatedly
not: is a request the receiver sends on a timer to check for news

cards.subject: A webhook endpoint
says: is a URL the receiver exposes to accept deliveries
should answer quickly with a 2xx status
cards.use: need a place for a provider to send events
not: is the URL of the sender's API

cards.subject: A webhook signature
says: lets the receiver verify the sender with a shared-secret HMAC
is computed over the request body
cards.use: need to confirm that a request really came from the provider
not: encrypts the payload so nobody on the wire can read it

cards.subject: Fast acknowledgement
says: returns a 2xx first and does the real work afterwards
keeps slow processing from causing sender timeouts and duplicate retries
cards.use: see a provider time out and redeliver while your handler is still working
not: finishes all processing before replying

cards.subject: At-least-once webhook delivery
says: can send the same event twice
treats a missing or non-2xx response as a reason to retry
cards.use: must build a receiver that survives duplicate deliveries
not: promises each event arrives exactly one time

cards.subject: Webhook replay protection
says: rejects deliveries whose signed timestamp is too old
keeps a captured delivery from being resent later
cards.use: worry that an attacker could resend a captured delivery
not: is achieved by hiding the endpoint URL

cards.subject: Raw-body verification
says: computes the signature over the exact bytes received
fails if a framework re-serialises the JSON before checking
cards.use: see valid signatures fail after a middleware parses the body
not: verifies the signature over the parsed JSON object

cards.subject: Subscription auto-pause
says: stops sending to an endpoint after sustained failures
protects the sender from hammering a dead URL
cards.use: see a subscriber's endpoint fail on every delivery for days
not: deletes the subscription's history

cards.subject: Idempotency
says: makes repeating an operation have the same effect as doing it once
is what makes retries safe
cards.use: need a retry not to charge a customer twice
not: guarantees an operation is never attempted more than once

cards.subject: An idempotency key
says: is a client-supplied unique id stored with the first result
lets a repeated request return the saved response instead of redoing the work
cards.use: need to make a POST that creates something safe to retry
not: is a server-generated session cookie

cards.subject: A retry
says: repeats a failed operation in the hope the cause was temporary
helps with transient faults but is pointless for permanent ones
cards.use: see a call fail with a brief network blip
not: fixes a request that was malformed

cards.subject: Exponential backoff
says: increases the wait between retries, typically doubling it
gives a struggling dependency room to recover
cards.use: see retries hammering a service that is already overloaded
not: retries at a fixed interval forever

cards.subject: Jitter
says: adds randomness to retry delays
stops many clients retrying at the same instant
cards.use: see a thundering herd after an outage ends
not: lengthens every delay by the same fixed amount

cards.subject: A dead-letter queue
says: holds messages that exhausted their retries
lets a person inspect and redrive failures
keeps a failing message from blocking healthy ones
cards.use: need failed jobs parked for inspection
not: permanently deletes failed messages to keep the queue clean

cards.subject: A poison message
says: fails every time it is processed
will clog a queue if it is retried for ever
cards.use: find one malformed message stuck at the head of a queue
not: succeeds on the second attempt

cards.subject: A circuit breaker
says: stops calls to a dependency after repeated failures
moves between closed, open and half-open states
cards.use: see calls piling up against a failing service
not: retries every failed call immediately

cards.subject: A timeout
says: gives up on a call that takes too long
turns a hung call into a failure that retry policy can handle
cards.use: have a call that can hang with no answer
not: makes a slow call finish faster

cards.subject: A transient error
says: is expected to clear by itself
is the kind of fault a retry can fix, such as a 503
cards.use: see a dependency briefly unavailable
not: will fail the same way however many times it is repeated

cards.subject: A permanent error
says: will not succeed however often it is retried
is shown by a validation failure such as a 400 for a bad field
cards.use: get a rejection for a payload that is malformed
not: clears up after a short wait

cards.subject: At-least-once delivery
says: may deliver a message more than once but never loses it
is the usual broker default that leaves duplicate handling to the consumer
cards.use: must choose a delivery guarantee where loss is unacceptable
not: promises no message is ever delivered twice

cards.subject: Exactly-once processing
says: is achieved in practice by at-least-once delivery plus idempotent handling
is a property of the outcome rather than of the network
cards.use: need each payment to take effect one time despite redeliveries
not: is provided by every broker with no consumer work

cards.subject: A cron expression
says: describes a recurring time with five fields
reads minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week
cards.use: need to say 'every weekday at 08:30'
not: names a single moment that happens only once

cards.subject: A scheduler
says: starts work at defined times or intervals
turns a time rule into queued jobs
cards.use: need a task to start without anyone clicking
not: decides how a job's steps are ordered

cards.subject: A delayed job
says: runs once at a chosen future time
is created when something happens but executes later
cards.use: need to send a reminder 24 hours after sign-up
not: repeats on a cron schedule for ever

cards.subject: A fixed-rate schedule
says: starts runs at regular clock intervals regardless of how long they take
can start a new run while the previous one is still going
cards.use: need a report every 10 minutes on the clock
not: waits a set time after the previous run finishes

cards.subject: A fixed-delay schedule
says: waits a set time after the previous run finishes
never lets two runs overlap
cards.use: need a gap between the end of one run and the start of the next
not: starts runs at regular clock times whatever the duration

cards.subject: A schedule time zone
says: fixes a schedule to an explicit zone
matters because daylight saving shifts skip or repeat local hours
cards.use: see a 02:30 job vanish on the night the clocks change
not: is irrelevant when a schedule runs once a day

cards.subject: An overlap policy
says: decides what happens when a run is still going at the next tick
offers choices such as skip, queue or cancel the old run
cards.use: see a slow job still running when the next run is due
not: decides which time zone a schedule uses

cards.subject: Misfire handling
says: decides whether runs missed during downtime are skipped or run late
bounds how many missed runs are caught up
cards.use: restart a scheduler after a long outage
not: retries a failed run immediately

cards.subject: A scheduler lock
says: ensures only one instance fires a schedule
prevents duplicate runs when several scheduler instances are deployed
cards.use: see a cron job fire twice after scaling to two instances
not: lets every instance run the schedule for safety

cards.subject: A dead man's switch
says: alerts when an expected run does not check in
catches a job that silently stopped running
cards.use: worry that a nightly job has quietly stopped
not: alerts only when a job reports an error

cards.subject: An approval gate
says: pauses a workflow until a person approves or rejects
records who decided and when
cards.use: need a person to sign off a payment above a limit
not: lets the workflow continue without waiting for anyone

cards.subject: Human in the loop
says: keeps a person in the decision path of an automated process
ranges from approving every item to sampling a few
cards.use: want people to stay accountable for automated outcomes
not: removes every person from the process

cards.subject: An audit trail
says: records who or what decided, with the inputs and the time
lets a decision be reconstructed later
cards.use: need to explain months later why something was approved
not: stores only the final outcome without inputs

cards.subject: A confidence threshold
says: routes low-confidence machine decisions to a person
is best set from measured error rates
cards.use: want the machine to decide only when it is sure
not: is a fixed value that is never reviewed

cards.subject: A sampling audit
says: reviews a fixed fraction of confident automated decisions
catches silent drift in a model that looks accurate
cards.use: worry that a once-accurate classifier is now failing quietly
not: reviews only the decisions the machine was unsure about

cards.subject: A four-eyes rule
says: requires two different people to approve a sensitive action
prevents the requester approving their own request
cards.use: need a payout to be approved by someone other than its author
not: lets one person approve any request at any size

cards.subject: An escalation
says: passes a stalled approval to a more senior person after a time limit
keeps a request from sitting unanswered
cards.use: see an approval request sit unanswered for days
not: cancels the request when nobody answers

cards.subject: Automation bias
says: leads reviewers to accept machine suggestions without checking
reduces the value of an approval gate
cards.use: see approvers accept every suggestion within seconds
not: makes people distrust every machine suggestion

cards.subject: Override capture
says: records when a person changes a machine decision
turns corrections into data for improving the automation
cards.use: want human corrections to cut future human work
not: blocks people from changing machine decisions

cards.subject: A reject option
says: lets a classifier abstain instead of guess
trades coverage for lower error on the cases it does answer
cards.use: need a classifier to hand uncertain cases to a person
not: forces a label on every input however unclear

cards.subject: A reusable pattern
says: captures a proven solution to a recurring problem
is applied by adapting it rather than copying it unchanged
cards.use: face a problem that others have already solved well
not: is a one-off script written for a single customer

cards.subject: A template
says: is a pre-built workflow with blanks to fill in
gets someone started faster than a blank canvas
cards.use: want a new automation to start from a working example
not: is a finished automation that cannot be edited

cards.subject: Parameterisation
says: exposes the few settings that vary between uses
keeps the logic fixed while the values change
cards.use: need the same logic with different thresholds for different teams
not: copies the logic and edits it for each team

cards.subject: Composition
says: builds larger behaviour by combining small units
works best when each unit has clear inputs and outputs
cards.use: want big automations made from small tested parts
not: relies on one very large unit that does everything

cards.subject: A typed contract
says: declares the input and output types of a unit
lets a composer check that steps fit together before running
cards.use: want a mismatch between two steps caught before it runs
not: leaves each unit's inputs undocumented

cards.subject: Versioned revisions
says: let a change ship without silently altering every consumer
allow a consumer to pin a version and roll back
cards.use: need to change a shared unit without breaking its users
not: overwrite the single live copy in place

cards.subject: A registry
says: lists available units with their versions and owners
makes reuse discoverable
cards.use: find that two teams built the same automation unaware of each other
not: runs the units on behalf of the callers

cards.subject: Reusing a published algorithm
says: inherits years of scrutiny and known behaviour
needs its source and licence to be recorded
cards.use: need a well-understood method rather than a home-made one
not: avoids having to test the implementation

cards.subject: Shadow mode
says: runs a new automation beside the old path without acting on its output
compares the two results before any switch
cards.use: want to test replacing a manual process safely
not: switches all traffic to the new path at once

cards.subject: A strangler migration
says: replaces a legacy path piece by piece
retires old code as each piece is switched over
cards.use: need to replace a large legacy system without a big-bang cutover
not: keeps the old and new paths running side by side for ever

cards.subject: Polling
says: asks a system repeatedly whether anything changed
wastes calls when changes are rare
cards.use: must work with a system that offers no webhooks
not: waits for the other system to call back

cards.subject: An adapter
says: translates between one system's interface and another's
keeps vendor quirks out of core logic
cards.use: want to swap a vendor without rewriting the business logic
not: stores a copy of the vendor's whole database

cards.subject: An automation hub
says: connects many apps through prebuilt connectors and generic webhook and HTTP steps
lets a non-developer chain apps together
cards.use: want a no-code way to connect a trigger in one app to an action in another
not: replaces the need for any API on the apps

cards.subject: File interchange
says: moves data as an exported file such as JSON, Markdown or CSV
works with systems that offer no API
cards.use: need to hand data to a system that has no API
not: pushes data to the system in real time

cards.subject: Pagination
says: returns large results in pages
requires the client to ask for each following page
cards.use: see an API return only the first hundred records
not: returns every record in one response however many exist

cards.subject: Cursor pagination
says: continues from an opaque position token
stays stable when rows are inserted during paging
cards.use: see rows duplicated or skipped while paging a live list
not: jumps to an arbitrary page number

cards.subject: Rate-limit handling
says: backs off when the API answers 429
reads a Retry-After header where one is offered
cards.use: see an API reject calls with a 429
not: retries instantly until the call succeeds

cards.subject: An OpenAPI document
says: describes an HTTP API's operations and schemas in machine-readable form
allows clients and connectors to be generated
cards.use: want connectors and client code generated for an HTTP API
not: is the running code of the API

cards.subject: An MCP server
says: exposes tools and data to an AI assistant through a standard protocol
lets one assistant integration work across many compatible clients
cards.use: want an AI assistant to call your tools through a standard interface
not: is a database engine for vector search

cards.subject: A canonical data model
says: defines one shared shape that every system maps to
reduces N-by-N mappings to N
cards.use: must connect many systems that each speak a different format
not: maps each pair of systems directly

cards.subject: An anti-corruption layer
says: stops a foreign system's concepts leaking into your domain model
translates at the boundary in both directions
cards.use: worry that a legacy vendor's data model is spreading through your code
not: merges both systems into one shared database

cards.subject: A runbook
says: documents the steps for handling a known failure
lets whoever is on call act without guessing
cards.use: need a clear procedure for a failure that has happened before
not: is the code that fixes the failure automatically

cards.subject: A dry run
says: reports what an automation would do without doing it
lets a rule be checked against real data safely
cards.use: want to check what a new rule would change before enabling it
not: performs the changes and then reports them

cards.subject: A kill switch
says: stops an automation at once without a deploy
is kept simple enough to use under pressure
cards.use: see an automation misfiring at scale
not: waits for the next release to take effect

cards.subject: A correlation id
says: follows one request across every service and log line
lets a failed run be traced end to end
cards.use: need to trace a failed run across several services
not: identifies the user's account for billing

cards.subject: Queue depth and age
says: shows backlog growth before users notice
gives the oldest waiting item's age as the more telling signal
cards.use: want an early warning that workers are falling behind
not: reports only how many jobs succeeded

cards.subject: A blast radius limit
says: caps how much one automation can change in a single run
turns a buggy rule into a small incident rather than a large one
cards.use: worry that a buggy rule could delete thousands of records
not: removes the need to test the rule

cards.subject: An automation rate
says: measures the share of cases completed without a person
is trustworthy only when counted from recorded decisions rather than estimated
cards.use: want to know how much of the work the machine really does
not: counts only the cases a person reviewed

cards.subject: A Moksy pattern
says: is one decision with an id, typed inputs and outputs, bounded parameters and versioned revisions
is the unit that a flow is built from
cards.use: need to name a single smart decision inside Moksy
not: is a whole customer journey from idea to blueprint

cards.subject: A Moksy flow
says: is a set of patterns and flows with named exports
is itself a step, so patterns combine into bigger patterns
has its order derived by topological sort rather than written by hand
cards.use: need to name a group of patterns that together decide something larger
not: is a single decision with no other patterns inside it

cards.subject: The 1:99 goal
says: asks for 99 percent of the work to be done by machine and 1 percent by a human
is measured from recorded decisions rather than guessed
cards.use: want to state the founder's target for machine versus human work
not: asks for one human per ninety-nine customers

cards.subject: The decidedBy stamp
says: marks every dispatch as machine or human
is the data from which the 1:99 share is summed
cards.use: need to know how Moksy counts who made each decision
not: records which customer asked for the decision

cards.subject: The pattern dispatcher
says: runs a pattern and stamps who decided
keeps a revision manifest of what ran
cards.use: need the component that runs patterns and records the run
not: only lists which patterns exist

cards.subject: A selection shape
says: describes how a pattern decides, such as classify, cover, configure, retrieve, derive, trigger or attach
returns a because alongside its answer
makes a new dataset a table rather than a release
cards.use: need to say how a Moksy pattern arrives at its choice
not: is a visual layout used by the dashboard

cards.subject: The because field
says: explains a pattern's decision in words a person can read
lets a person see, and so correct, a decision
cards.use: want a decision to be visible and correctable
not: hides the reason for a decision to protect the algorithm

cards.subject: The pattern registry
says: declares the patterns and flows of the pattern architecture
separates patterns declared from patterns implemented
cards.use: need to know how many patterns exist and how many actually run
not: executes each pattern when a customer asks

cards.subject: Pattern provenance
says: requires each implementation to name the published algorithm it stands on
counts unnamed implementations in a number that can only fall
cards.use: need to know where a Moksy decision's method came from
not: lets any implementation skip naming its method

cards.subject: PatternRunService
says: is the run seam for patterns
is admin-only and deliberately not on the customer path
cards.use: need to know why admins can run patterns but customers' live decisions do not use them
not: serves every customer decision in the live interview

cards.subject: The 51-decision brief
says: traces each of the founder's 51 lines to the patterns that would decide it
marks each decision as inline, mixed, modelOnly or none
cards.use: want to see which decisions still run outside patterns
not: lists 51 patterns that are already live

cards.subject: The live-path reading of 0 percent
says: came from the live interview deciding inline in a large service file rather than through the dispatcher
meant no human share could yet be computed
cards.use: must explain why the brief did not claim 1:99 as a result
not: showed that machines made no decisions at all

cards.subject: The Blueprint flow
says: needs nothing from outside except run context
stands for the whole path from idea to Blueprint
cards.use: need the flow that covers an entire idea-to-Blueprint run
not: needs another flow's output before it can start

cards.subject: The never handoff mode
says: leaves the machine as the final decider
is declared on badges, level, ranking and level changes
cards.use: need the mode where no person ever decides
not: sends every case to a person

cards.subject: The onDoubt handoff mode
says: hands a decision to a person when the output itself says it is unsure
is the default for patterns that declare nothing else
cards.use: need the default mode where a person decides only when the machine doubts
not: audits a fixed share of confident answers as well

cards.subject: The sample handoff mode
says: adds a fixed audit rate to onDoubt for confident answers
draws deterministically by hashing the run key so a replay routes identically
cards.use: need audits of confident machine answers that replay the same way
not: has a person approve a whole batch once

cards.subject: The batch handoff mode
says: has the machine decide every row and a person approve the batch once
counts as one human touch rather than one per row
cards.use: need the monthly MXP to MOX close approved in one go
not: sends each row to a different person

cards.subject: The always handoff mode
says: makes a person decide while the machine writes the case file
is declared for accreditation grants and choosing who to hire
cards.use: need the mode where a person always decides
not: leaves the machine as the final decider

cards.subject: A Moksy confidence floor
says: sets the confidence below which a decision goes to a person
is hand-set today at 0.6 for customer-facing and 0.35 for internal decisions
cards.use: need the numbers behind the onDoubt hand-off
not: is learned automatically from every override today

cards.subject: Pattern coverage
says: is the share of decisions that went through a pattern at all
shows a decision still made inline as unpublished
cards.use: want to know how much of the work can be seen by the ledger
not: is the share of pattern decisions that needed no person

cards.subject: Machine share
says: is the share of pattern decisions that needed no person
counts a batch approval once rather than once per row
cards.use: want the number the 1:99 target is judged by
not: is the share of decisions that went through a pattern at all

cards.subject: meetsTarget
says: is true only when machine share is at least 0.99 and nothing is unmanaged
stays false while any decision is made outside the patterns
cards.use: need to know when the ledger will say the 1:99 goal is met
not: is true as soon as machine share reaches 0.99 on its own

cards.subject: The worst ranking
says: ranks patterns by the human time they cost
is the build backlog for the next patterns to automate
cards.use: need to choose which pattern to automate next
not: lists the patterns with the most errors

cards.subject: Conformal risk control
says: is the designed next step for setting each floor from confirmed versus overridden outcomes
bounds the human share by construction rather than by hope
cards.use: want confidence floors set from evidence rather than by hand
not: is how the floors are set today

cards.subject: Moksy's grounding rule
says: lets a model phrase a figure but never originate one
makes the system refuse, ask, derive or give a band when a fact is missing
cards.use: need the guardrail on numbers a machine shows a customer
not: lets a model estimate any number that is missing

cards.subject: The Moksy integration catalogue
says: covers 1,165 apps in 41 families
is derived from one line per app, family and recipe
reaches apps by one of 13 paths over ten primitives
cards.use: need the size and shape of Moksy's integration claims
not: is a list of apps with a native adapter each

cards.subject: Moksy webhook events
says: include blueprint.ready, review.submitted and review.verdict
let an outside app be told when a Blueprint or a review lands
cards.use: want a chat channel told the moment a Blueprint is ready
not: are sent only by email

cards.subject: The Moksy-Signature header
says: carries a timestamp t and a v1 HMAC-SHA256 of the timestamp, a dot and the raw body
is checked by a receiver, who rejects a timestamp more than five minutes off
cards.use: need to verify that a Moksy delivery is genuine and fresh
not: is a bearer token that gives access to the Moksy API

cards.subject: The Moksy webhook retry schedule
says: makes eight attempts over about three days
widens the wait between attempts and adds about ten percent jitter
cards.use: need to know how long a receiver has to recover before Moksy gives up
not: retries once and then drops the event

cards.subject: A Moksy API key
says: is created in Settings under API and webhooks
lets an outside tool call the operations in the OpenAPI document
cards.use: need an outside script or hub step to call Moksy
not: is the customer's login password

cards.subject: The Moksy MCP server
says: is shipped as @moksy/mcp-server
uses a propose then confirm step on every tool that writes
cards.use: want an AI assistant to read Blueprints and run a briefing
not: lets an assistant write without any confirmation

cards.subject: Moksy hub paths
says: reach Zapier, n8n, Make, Pipedream and Power Automate through generic webhook and HTTP steps
need only a Moksy API key until a Moksy app is published on the hub
cards.use: want to connect Moksy to an app through a no-code hub
not: require a native Moksy adapter for every app

cards.subject: Moksy integration effort grades
says: rate E0 as needing nothing beyond the page and recipe
rate E1 as a hub template or worked API example
rate E2 as a native adapter with consent, mapping and sealed tokens
cards.use: need to judge how much work an integration takes
not: rate every integration as needing a native adapter

cards.subject: The Moksy jobs states
says: are scheduled, queued, running, completed, failed, canceled and paused
let a running job move only to completed or failed
cards.use: need to know which transitions the Moksy jobs service allows
not: let a running job be paused or canceled

cards.subject: The Moksy jobs failure path
says: retries a worker failure with backoff until attempts are exhausted
dead-letters the job when the attempts run out
clears the attempt count when a failed job is manually retried
cards.use: need to follow what happens to a Moksy job that keeps failing
not: drops a failed job silently after one attempt

cards.subject: The Moksy events service
says: persists webhook subscriptions and signs each delivery
keeps a delivery log and can replay a delivery by id
cards.use: need the Moksy service that sends outbound webhooks
not: holds the subscriber list only in process memory

cards.subject: The Moksy event target design
says: puts a durable broker behind events, with Redis Streams named as the pragmatic choice
pairs it with the transactional outbox, retries and a dead-letter queue
cards.use: need the architecture review's target for event delivery
not: keeps events as inline HTTP calls with no retry

cards.subject: The Moksy three rules
says: use synchronous calls only when the caller needs the answer
make everything else an event written through an outbox
require every cross-service interface to be a published contract
cards.use: need the architecture review's definition of done for service calls
not: allow every service to call every other directly

cards.subject: The Moksy outbox finding
says: found the outbox only in the communications service
noted that the pattern existed in the repository but was not the platform default
cards.use: need to recall where the review found the outbox pattern in use
not: found an outbox in every service

cards.subject: A Moksy real-jobs test run
says: walks one real job post end to end through each role
goes both in and out as customer, reviewer, staff and account manager
cards.use: want to test the whole platform with one realistic case
not: checks one database table row by row

cards.subject: The Moksy manual deploy
says: is run by pulling on the server and running npm run deploy:prod
rebuilds only changed services, health-checks and records the commit

not: happens automatically when code is pushed to GitHub

qa.q: What does a webhook do that polling does not?
qa.right: The sender calls the receiver when an event happens
wrong: The receiver asks the sender every few seconds
The receiver downloads a nightly export
The sender waits for the receiver to log in
qa.why: A webhook is a push: the sender makes an HTTP call when the event occurs, so the receiver does not have to ask repeatedly.

qa.q: Which cron expression means 'at 08:30 every weekday'?
qa.why: Cron fields are minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week, so 08:30 on Monday to Friday is 30 8 * * 1-5.

qa.q: What is the 1:99 goal in Moksy's pattern architecture?
qa.right: 99 percent of the work done by machine and 1 percent by a human
wrong: One human reviewer for every 99 customers
99 percent uptime with one outage a quarter
qa.why: The brief states the founder's goal as 1:99, measured from the decidedBy stamp on every dispatch.

qa.q: Which name is in the Moksy webhook event list?
qa.right: blueprint.ready
qa.why: The integration catalogue lists blueprint.ready, review.submitted and review.verdict as webhook events.

qa.q: In Moksy, what does every selection shape return alongside its answer?
qa.right: A because
qa.why: Every shape returns a because so a person can see and correct the decision.

qa.q: What does a dead-letter queue hold?
qa.right: Messages that exhausted their retries
wrong: Messages waiting for their first attempt
Messages that arrived out of order
qa.why: A dead-letter queue parks messages that could not be processed after the allowed attempts, for inspection and redrive.

qa.q: A cron job should run at 02:30 local time in a zone with daylight saving. What can go wrong?
qa.right: On the night the clocks move forward the local 02:30 may not exist, so the run is skipped or shifted
wrong: The job runs every minute that night
The job runs only on leap years
qa.why: Daylight saving can skip or repeat local hours, so a schedule needs an explicit zone and a rule for those nights.

qa.q: Which of these is a command rather than an event?
qa.right: ChargeCustomer
qa.why: A command asks a specific recipient to do something and is named in the imperative; events are past-tense facts.

qa.q: A Moksy flow is a set of patterns and flows. What else is a flow?
qa.right: Itself a step, so flows can be combined into bigger ones
wrong: A single decision with no inner steps
qa.why: The brief says a flow is itself a step, so patterns combine into bigger patterns.

qa.q: What is wrong with this retry loop for a 503 from a struggling API?
qa.right: It retries at once with no delay, which adds load to a service that is already overloaded
wrong: It retries too few times to ever succeed
It should retry only on 200 responses
qa.why: Retries need a wait that grows (backoff), ideally with jitter, so they do not hammer a dependency that needs room to recover.

qa.q: Why does this retry delay still cause a thundering herd after an outage?
qa.right: Every client waits exactly the same time, so they all retry together
wrong: Math.pow cannot be used for delays
The delay is applied before the first attempt
qa.why: Without jitter, clients that failed together retry together. Add randomness to each delay.
qa.code:
const delay = 1000 * Math.pow(2, attempt);
await sleep(delay);

qa.q: A client sends this request twice after a timeout. What should the server do on the second call?
qa.right: Return the stored response of the first call and not create a second order
wrong: Create a second order with a new id
Reject it with 500 because the key was seen before
Delete the first order and recreate it
qa.why: The Idempotency-Key header lets the server save the first result and answer a repeat with it, so retries are safe.

qa.q: Which line of this webhook receiver is the bug?
qa.right: Parsing the body with express.json() before verifying, so the signature is checked over re-serialised JSON
qa.why: Signatures are computed over the exact bytes received. Verify against the raw body before parsing.

qa.q: What does this crontab line do?
qa.right: Runs the backup script at 02:15 on the first day of each month
wrong: Runs the backup script every 15 minutes
Runs the backup script at 02:15 every day
Runs the backup script on the 15th at 02:00
qa.why: Fields are minute 15, hour 2, day of month 1, any month, any weekday.

qa.q: Given these job states, which transition does the rule table forbid?
qa.right: running to queued
qa.why: Only completed or failed may follow running in this table. A state machine rejects any move not declared.

qa.q: What does a receiver compute for the Moksy-Signature header with this form?
qa.right: An HMAC-SHA256 of the timestamp, a dot and the raw body, using the shared secret
wrong: A SHA-1 hash of the body alone
An RSA signature of the header itself
A base64 copy of the secret
qa.why: The delivery code documents that the timestamp is inside the signed string, so a captured delivery cannot be replayed with a fresh header.

qa.q: Why does the signed timestamp t matter in this header?
qa.right: A receiver can reject a delivery whose t is more than five minutes from now, defeating replay
wrong: It tells the receiver which time zone the sender uses
It is how the receiver orders events
qa.why: The timestamp sits inside the signed string, so it cannot be changed, and an old delivery fails the freshness check.

qa.q: What happens to the third item of this pipeline when the second fails, in a saga?
qa.right: The compensating action of the first item runs, and the third item never starts
wrong: The database rolls back all three automatically
The first item is retried until the second succeeds
qa.why: A saga undoes completed local steps with compensations because there is no shared transaction.
qa.code:
1. reserve stock   (compensate: release stock)
2. charge card     (compensate: refund)
3. book courier    (compensate: cancel booking)

qa.q: A scheduler runs on two replicas and a nightly job fires twice. Which fix addresses the cause?
qa.right: Add a scheduler lock or leader election so only one instance fires the schedule
wrong: Add jitter to the retry delay
qa.why: Duplicate fires come from several scheduler instances; only one should own the schedule.

qa.q: What does this outbox sequence guarantee?
qa.right: The state change and the event row commit together or not at all, so the event is never lost
wrong: The event is delivered exactly once
The consumer processes events in global order
The broker never needs a retry
qa.why: The relay publishes stored rows afterwards, which gives at-least-once delivery. Consumers must still handle duplicates.

qa.q: A team's webhook handler does all its work before replying. The provider keeps redelivering the same event. What should the team do first?
qa.right: Acknowledge with 2xx straight away, queue the work, and make the handler idempotent
qa.why: Slow handlers time out the sender, which retries. Reply fast, process afterwards, and tolerate duplicates.

qa.q: A nightly import fails for one record with a 400 on a bad field. The job retries it 8 times. What is the better design?
qa.right: Treat a 400 as a permanent error, send that record to a dead letter, and carry on
wrong: Retry it more slowly for longer
Switch the 400 to a 503 so retry works
qa.why: Retrying a permanent error cannot help. Park it for a person and keep the rest moving.

qa.q: A queue's oldest message is 40 minutes old while the depth is small. What does this most likely show?
qa.right: A stuck or poison message at the head, not a throughput shortage
qa.why: A small depth with a large age points to something blocking, so check for a message failing repeatedly.

qa.q: A bulk import is exhausting the database connection pool and slowing the website. What is the most direct fix?
qa.right: Put a concurrency limit on the import job
wrong: Add jitter to the import schedule
qa.why: A concurrency limit caps how many jobs of one kind run at once and protects the downstream system.

qa.q: A team sets an approval gate for every refund. Approvers now click approve within seconds on all items. What is the risk, and what helps?
qa.right: Automation bias has emptied the gate; add sampling, show the reason and measure rejection rates
wrong: Nothing; fast approvals mean the gate works
The approvers are too slow, so remove the gate
The gate needs more approvers per item
qa.why: A gate that is always passed protects nothing. Surface the reasoning and track how often people disagree.

qa.q: A classifier is accurate in testing but quietly drifting in production. Which control would catch it?
qa.right: A sampling audit of confident decisions
qa.why: Confident answers bypass the person, so only a fixed audit rate on them reveals silent drift.

qa.q: A team wants to replace a manual triage process with an automated rule. What is the safest first step?
qa.right: Run the rule in shadow mode beside the manual process and compare results
wrong: Switch off the manual process and watch for complaints
Run it on 5 percent of cases with no comparison
Ask users whether they like it
qa.why: Shadow mode acts on nothing and gives evidence of agreement before any switch.

qa.q: Two teams discover they both built an address-cleaning automation. What would have prevented the duplicate?
qa.right: A registry of reusable units with owners and versions
wrong: A rule that every step needs a retry
qa.why: Reuse needs discoverability; a registry lists what exists so teams adopt rather than rebuild.

qa.q: A webhook subscriber's endpoint has returned errors for three days. What should the sender do?
qa.right: Back off, then pause the subscription and tell the owner, keeping a delivery log for replay
wrong: Retry every second until it works
Send the events to a different customer's endpoint
qa.why: Pausing protects both sides; the log lets the owner replay once the endpoint is fixed.

qa.q: A job takes 40 minutes but the visibility timeout is 5 minutes. What will happen?
qa.right: Another worker will claim the job and it will run twice, unless a heartbeat extends the claim
wrong: The job will be cancelled with no retry
Nothing; the timeout only applies to failed jobs
qa.why: A claim that expires while the job is still running returns it to the queue. Heartbeats or a longer claim fix this.

qa.q: A process is described as automated, yet every case goes to a person for approval. How should its machine share be reported?
qa.right: As mostly human, because the share is counted from who decided, not what is claimed
wrong: As 99 percent machine, since the design is automated
As 50 percent because both are involved
qa.why: Moksy's approach stamps each dispatch as machine or human and sums those rows, so the share cannot be claimed by design.

qa.q: A team proposes to switch a Moksy pattern from onDoubt to never to raise the machine share. What should you check first?
qa.right: Whether errors are costly enough that a person must stay able to catch them, since never removes the exit
wrong: Whether the pattern has a because
Whether the job queue is empty
qa.why: never makes the machine final, so it fits low-risk decisions like badges and rankings, not ones with serious consequences.

qa.q: A finance process uses batch approval for the month-end close. A reviewer proposes counting each row as a human touch. What is the effect?
qa.right: It would inflate the human share, because a batch approval is counted once, not once per row
wrong: It would raise the machine share
qa.why: In Moksy's ledger a batch approval counts once; the machine decided every row and a person approved the batch.

qa.q: A migration plan runs both an inline function and a pattern for the same decision indefinitely. Why is this a problem?
qa.right: Two ways to run a step is worse than one, so the inline path should be deleted when the switch happens
wrong: It is cheaper than the alternative
It is the intended long-term design
qa.why: The migration rule is that each phase ends with the inline code deleted, so only one path remains.

qa.q: Which of these counts as the data behind Moksy's machine share?
qa.right: The machine or human value stamped on each dispatch
wrong: The number of patterns in the registry
qa.why: The share is the sum of decidedBy rows, so it is measured rather than estimated.

qa.q: According to the brief, what did the live customer interview use to decide, as of 2026-09-14?
qa.right: Inline code in a large service file, not the dispatcher
wrong: The pattern dispatcher for every decision
A human reviewer for every decision
qa.why: The brief says the live path decides inline, so measured coverage was 0 percent.

qa.q: Which pair is correctly matched for Moksy's handoff modes?
qa.right: batch with the monthly MXP to MOX close
qa.why: The monthly close has the machine decide every row and a person approve once.

qa.q: What is a Moksy selection shape?
qa.right: A way a pattern decides, such as classify or retrieve
wrong: A way to draw a report
qa.why: The seven shapes are classify, cover, configure, retrieve, derive, trigger and attach.

qa.q: Which pairing for coverage and machine share is right in Moksy's ledger?
qa.right: Coverage is the share of decisions through a pattern; machine share is the share of pattern decisions needing no person
wrong: Coverage counts human decisions; machine share counts patterns
They are two names for the same number
Coverage is measured only for batch decisions
qa.why: They fail differently: an inline decision is invisible to machine share, which only sees pattern decisions.

qa.q: When is meetsTarget true in Moksy's ledger?
qa.right: When machine share is at least 0.99 and nothing is unmanaged
wrong: When machine share is at least 0.5
When the dispatcher has no errors
qa.why: Both conditions are required, so a high share with unmanaged decisions still fails.

qa.q: A founder asks whether a pattern's decision can be shown to a customer with a reason. Which Moksy feature provides it?
qa.right: The because that every selection shape returns
qa.why: The because explains the decision so a person can see and correct it.

qa.q: In the Moksy jobs service, which states can a failed job move to?
qa.right: queued, canceled or paused
qa.why: A failed job can be queued again, canceled or paused, but not marked completed directly.

qa.q: How long, roughly, does Moksy keep retrying a failing webhook delivery?
qa.right: About three days over eight attempts
wrong: About ten seconds over two attempts
About a month over a hundred attempts
qa.why: The delivery code states a backoff of about three days over eight attempts.

qa.q: A customer-facing figure in a Moksy report is missing from the data. What does the grounding rule say the system should do?
qa.right: Refuse, ask, derive from data, or give a band, but never have a model invent the number
wrong: Let the model estimate it quietly
qa.why: A model may phrase a figure but may never originate one.

qa.q: Why does Moksy's brief say 1:99 is achievable only as a measured number?
qa.right: Because every decision must go through the dispatcher and be stamped before a share can be computed
wrong: Because it needs a new database
qa.why: While decisions are made inline, they are invisible to the ledger.

qa.q: Which Moksy construct is meant to bound the human share by construction rather than by hand-set floors?
qa.right: Conformal risk control over confirmed versus overridden outcomes
qa.why: The brief names conformal risk control as the designed next step for setting each floor from outcomes.

qa.q: Which Moksy integration path would a team choose to pass a Blueprint to an app that has no API and no webhook support?
qa.right: The Blueprint interchange file in Markdown, JSON, HTML or PDF
wrong: A native adapter with sealed tokens
qa.why: File interchange needs nothing from the app side but a place to open or paste a file.

qa.q: The architecture review said a restart mid-report killed work permanently. What cause and cure did it give?
qa.right: Events were sent by inline HTTP with no queue or retry; use a broker plus a transactional outbox with retry and a dead-letter queue
wrong: Reports were too large; split them into pages
Workers had too little memory; add RAM
Cron was misconfigured; fix the timezone
qa.why: Without a durable queue a delivery lost to a restart is lost. The cure is durable delivery with replay.
